pr_title: HTTP/3: Disable HTTP/3 when multiple protocols used on dynamic port

issue_context.title: HTTP/3: Ephemeral port and connection already in use
issue_context.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

A set of ASP.NET Core HTTP/3 tests failed - https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/42967. They are both configured to start on 127.0.0.1:0. Because the port is 0 (ephemeral) the listener should start on an unused port assigned by Windows.

Instead, this error is thrown: `System.Net.Quic.QuicException : The local address is already in use.`

The problem is Kestrel listening on HTTP/1.1 (TCP), HTTP/2 (TCP), and HTTP/3 (UDP).

The ephemeral port is used to bind a TCP socket first, which returns the assigned port. Then that port is reused with QUIC because we want the listener connections to share the same port number.

The problem is there's a chance that the free port for TCP is in use with UDP, causing this error.

### Expected Behavior

1. Kestrel starts up and is free from address in use errors.
2. The endpoint shares the same port numbers.

### Steps To Reproduce

Kestrel + epemeral port + HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3

The error will only happen if a TCP port is assigned and the same number UDP port is in use.

### Exceptions (if any)

`System.Net.Quic.QuicException : The local address is already in use.`

### .NET Version

_No response_

### Anything else?

_No response_
comments:
The current design tries to have a listener with multiple protocols and an ephemeral port use the port number. A simple solution is to allow different port numbers.

A solution that keeps the same port, but is kind of gross, is to put connection binding in a loop and keep retrying until both start successfully on the same port number.

What do IIS and httpsys do here?

The problem with allowing different port numbers is that you have no idea which port is TCP and UDP. `IServerAddressesFeature` gives a simple list of addresses without extra information about what each supports.

This reminds me how binding to "localhost:0" requires binding to both `127.0.0.1` and `::1` which has similar problems. We just [throw](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/6797f926dc6991294fb5e84505f13b672c2d97c6/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/LocalhostListenOptions.cs#L15-L18) in that case, and most people then just use ​`127.0.0.1:0`​ instead.

Not supporting port-zero binding for Http1AndHttp2AndHttp3 feels bad, but it's a niche enough use case that might be our best bet. If someone want to try binding to a random port and retry on failures in a loop, they can do that manually. Anything we did under the covers in this case would not be significantly better than that.

I'm not sure if throwing will work here. The eventual plan is to have `Http1AndHttp2AndHttp3` be the default. Anyone who uses port 0 and doesn't override the protocol will break when they upgrade to .NET vNext.

We could make binding 0 silently disable HTTP/3. Not ideal, but a log message on startup that explains why HTTP/3 is disabled could help anyone who is trying to do pre-negotiated HTTP/3.
Triage: log at Error level and add to docs.

review_comments: I probably would have just tried casting to an IPEndpoint and checked for port-0 up front, but I like this way of checking for dynamic binding.
Nit: I know other tests make use of this, but should we have a test specifically verifying port-0 binding works when just HTTP/3 is enabled?
I don't think it's necessary. Lots of tests rely on it working.
